_meta.keyKnowledge: We are learning to read and interpret graphs, models, and text to find patterns and trends in economic data.

toLevel2.question: A bar graph can show how the prices of common items have changed across the last ten years.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Bar graphs display values across categories and can compare prices across years.

distractors.explanation: Bar graphs are widely used to show prices changing across set time periods.

toLevel2.question: A pie chart has no link to showing how government spending is divided between different services.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A pie chart is a recognised way to show the share each service receives of total spending.

distractors.explanation: Treating pie charts as unrelated to spending splits ignores their core role at this level.

toLevel2.question: Spotting a trend in employment data can help a class predict what might happen next in that area.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Trends show direction over time, which supports predictions about likely future patterns.

distractors.explanation: Trend reading is widely taught as a basis for predicting likely future patterns.

toLevel2.question: A line graph of population growth has no link to showing how a population has changed across a period.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A line graph plots population values over time and reveals the shape of growth across the period.

distractors.explanation: Treating line graphs as unrelated to population change ignores their core role at this level.

toLevel2.question: Reading a data graph carefully has no link to understanding any economic information at any time.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Reading a graph carefully is the basis of understanding the economic information it shows.

distractors.explanation: Treating graphs as unrelated to information ignores how they show economic data.

toLevel2.question: A simple supply-and-demand model can help explain why some goods cost more than others in a market.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The supply-and-demand model links price to how much is supplied and how much is wanted.

distractors.explanation: This model is widely taught at this level as one explanation for price differences.

toLevel2.question: Comparing two graphs of different countries' economic data has no link to noting any differences.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Comparing two graphs reveals where the data agree and where they differ between countries.

distractors.explanation: Treating comparison as unrelated to noticing differences ignores its core purpose.

toLevel2.question: A pattern in data is something that repeats or stays steady across the values being shown.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A pattern is a repeating or steady feature in the data, such as a regular rise or fall.

distractors.explanation: This is the standard description of a pattern in economic data at this level.

toLevel2.question: A trend in employment data has no link to predicting how work might change in the years ahead.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: An employment trend gives a basis for predicting likely changes in work in the years ahead.

distractors.explanation: Treating trends as unrelated to predictions ignores their use in forecasting.

toLevel2.question: Interpretation skills used to read graphs and text have no link to economics or to daily decisions.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Reading graphs and text well supports decisions in economics and in everyday life.

distractors.explanation: Treating interpretation skills as unrelated to decisions ignores how widely they apply.

toLevel2.question: Reading a pie chart and reading a bar graph always produce exactly the same result for any data set.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Pie charts show shares of a whole; bar graphs compare values, so the two reveal different patterns.

distractors.explanation: Treating the two charts as identical ignores how each one displays different aspects of the data.

toLevel2.question: A line graph that rises steadily over years shows growth in the value being measured during the period.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A steadily rising line graph shows growth in the value being measured across the period.

distractors.explanation: Steadily rising lines are recognised as a basic graph reading of growth.

toLevel2.question: Why is a bar graph useful for showing how prices have changed over years?
toLevel2.correct: A bar graph compares values across categories and lets a reader see year-on-year price changes
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A bar graph compares values across categories and shows year-on-year price changes.

distractors.answer: A bar graph has no link to comparing any value across any category in any setting at any time
distractors.explanation: Bar graphs are directly linked to comparing values across categories.

distractors.answer: A bar graph always gives the same value for every category so no comparison is ever possible
distractors.explanation: Bar graphs show different values for different categories; comparison is possible.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following best describes a pie chart?
toLevel2.correct: A circular chart that shows the share each category takes of a single whole amount
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A pie chart is a circular chart that shows each category's share of a whole.

distractors.answer: A list of words that has no link to any chart, any whole amount, or any share at any time
distractors.explanation: A list of words is not a chart and does not show shares.

distractors.answer: A square chart that always shows exactly the same value for every category in every case
distractors.explanation: Pie charts are circular and show different shares; this option is wrong on both counts.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following best describes a trend in economic data?
toLevel2.correct: A clear direction in the data across many values that supports predictions about what may follow
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A trend is a clear direction across many values that supports predictions.

distractors.answer: A single one-off value that has no direction and has no link to any other value at any time
distractors.explanation: A one-off value with no direction is not a trend.

distractors.answer: A random scribble on a graph with no link to any value or to any reading of the data
distractors.explanation: A random scribble is not a meaningful reading of data.

toLevel2.question: What does a line graph of population growth most clearly show?
toLevel2.correct: The shape of population change across a chosen period of time, year by year
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A line graph of population shows the shape of change across a chosen period.

distractors.answer: The colour of every house in every town in every state of the country in every year
distractors.explanation: House colour has no link to population data on a line graph.

distractors.answer: The number of clouds passing over a single town during a quiet afternoon in autumn
distractors.explanation: Cloud counts have no link to population data on a line graph.

toLevel2.question: Why is a simple supply-and-demand model useful at this level?
toLevel2.correct: It links price to how much is supplied and how much is wanted in a market for a good
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The model links price to how much is supplied and how much is wanted in a market.

distractors.answer: It has no link to price, supply, or demand in any market at any time
distractors.explanation: The model is directly built around price, supply, and demand.

distractors.answer: It always gives the same price for every good no matter how much is supplied or wanted
distractors.explanation: Different supply and demand levels lead to different prices in the model.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following best illustrates spotting a pattern in data?
toLevel2.correct: Noticing that prices in a bar graph rise each year for the last five years in a row
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Noticing that prices rise each year for five years is a clear example of spotting a pattern.

distractors.answer: Counting how many trees grow in a park during the autumn months across one whole year
distractors.explanation: Counting trees has no link to spotting a pattern in economic data.

distractors.answer: Refusing to read any graph or any text and refusing to note any feature of any data
distractors.explanation: Refusing to read data is the opposite of spotting a pattern.

toLevel2.question: What is the main use of comparing two graphs of different countries' economic data?
toLevel2.correct: To find where the two patterns agree and where the two patterns differ across the period
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Comparing two graphs reveals where patterns agree and where they differ between countries.

distractors.answer: To prove that every country always has the same data on every economic measure in every year
distractors.explanation: Different countries usually have different economic data; identical data is rare.

distractors.answer: To refuse to read any graph and to claim that comparison has no link to economic data
distractors.explanation: Refusing to read graphs is the opposite of comparison.

toLevel2.question: Which scenario best shows reading a line graph for a trend?
toLevel2.correct: A class notes that the line on a population graph rises every year for the past ten years
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Noting that a line rises every year for ten years is a clear example of reading for a trend.

distractors.answer: A class refuses to look at any line graph and notes nothing about any trend at any time
distractors.explanation: Refusing to read graphs is the opposite of reading for a trend.

distractors.answer: A class counts how many leaves fall outside a school during the autumn months in any year
distractors.explanation: Counting leaves has no link to reading a line graph for a trend.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following is the best example of reading a pie chart?
toLevel2.correct: Noting which slice takes the largest share of total government spending in a single year
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Noting which slice takes the largest share is a clear example of reading a pie chart.

distractors.answer: Refusing to look at any slice on any pie chart at any time in any school
distractors.explanation: Refusing to look at slices is the opposite of reading a pie chart.

distractors.answer: Counting how many cars pass the school gate during the morning bell on a single Tuesday
distractors.explanation: Counting cars has no link to reading a pie chart of spending.

toLevel2.question: Which list includes only useful skills for reading economic data?
toLevel2.correct: Reading bar graphs, reading line graphs, reading pie charts, and spotting trends in text
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Reading bar graphs, line graphs, pie charts, and spotting trends in text are useful skills.

distractors.answer: Counting clouds, naming birds, painting walls, and timing the wind across many seasons
distractors.explanation: These activities have no link to reading economic data.

distractors.answer: Refusing to read graphs, refusing to read text, and refusing to spot any trend at any time
distractors.explanation: Refusing every reading task is the opposite of useful data-reading skills.

toLevel2.question: Why is interpretation a useful skill in everyday decision-making?
toLevel2.correct: Reading graphs and text well supports decisions about money, work, and many other choices
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Reading graphs and text well supports decisions about money, work, and many other choices.

distractors.answer: Reading graphs and text has no link to any decision about money, work, or any other choice
distractors.explanation: Interpretation is directly linked to decisions in many parts of life.

distractors.answer: Reading graphs and text always gives the same answer no matter what graph or text is read
distractors.explanation: Different graphs and text give different answers; interpretation is needed.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following is the best example of using a supply-and-demand model?
toLevel2.correct: Explaining why a popular product costs more when many buyers want a small available supply
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Explaining a price rise when demand outstrips supply is a clear use of the model.

distractors.answer: Counting clouds in the sky over a single shop on a single afternoon during the autumn months
distractors.explanation: Counting clouds has no link to a supply-and-demand explanation of price.

distractors.answer: Refusing to read any graph and refusing to use any model
distractors.explanation: Refusing to use any model is the opposite of using one.

toLevel3.question: A bar graph of bread, milk, and egg prices over ten years can reveal which item rose the most.
toLevel3.correct: True
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Bar graphs across years let a reader compare values and spot which item rose most over the period.

distractors.explanation: Bar graphs across years are widely used to compare price rises across products.

toLevel3.question: A pie chart showing government spending always shows the same slice size for every service in any year.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Spending shares vary by service and by year, so pie chart slices differ in size between services.

distractors.explanation: Treating slices as identical ignores how shares of spending vary widely between services and years.

toLevel3.question: A line graph showing more people working from home each year reveals an upward trend in that pattern of work.
toLevel3.correct: True
toLevel3.correctExplanation: A line that climbs each year reveals an upward trend in the value being measured across years.

distractors.explanation: Climbing lines on a line graph are recognised as upward trends in the data.

toLevel3.question: A simple supply-and-demand model has no link to explaining why some goods cost more than others in a market at any time.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: The supply-and-demand model links price to supply and demand and explains many price differences.

distractors.explanation: Treating the model as unrelated to price ignores its core role at this level.

toLevel3.question: Comparing two countries' line graphs of population has no link to spotting where the two patterns agree or differ.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Comparing two line graphs of population reveals where the two patterns agree and where they differ.

distractors.explanation: Treating the comparison as unrelated to spotting agreement and difference ignores its core purpose.

toLevel3.question: A trend in data is exactly the same idea as a single random one-off value with no direction at all.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: A trend is a direction across many values, while a one-off value has no direction by itself.

distractors.explanation: Treating trends as one-off values ignores how a trend describes direction across many points.

toLevel3.question: A reader who notices that prices on a bar graph rise each year is reading the graph for a clear price trend.
toLevel3.correct: True
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Noticing a rise each year on a price bar graph is reading the graph for a clear upward trend.

distractors.explanation: Year-on-year price rises are widely read as upward price trends in economic data.

toLevel3.question: A line graph that drops steadily across years has no link to any change in the value being measured at any time.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: A steadily dropping line shows that the value being measured has gone down across the years.

distractors.explanation: Treating a dropping line as unrelated to change ignores what the line is plotting.

toLevel3.question: Mia reads a bar graph of bread, milk, and egg prices over ten years. What is the best way to spot which item rose most?
toLevel3.correct: Compare each item's earliest bar with its latest bar and find the largest rise across the years
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Comparing each item's earliest and latest bars finds the largest rise across the years.

distractors.answer: Count bar colours and pick the brightest as the item that rose the most over the years
distractors.explanation: Bar colour does not show the size of a price rise.

distractors.answer: Refuse to read the bar graph and pick any item at random with no link to any of the data
distractors.explanation: Refusing to read the graph is the opposite of spotting a rise.

toLevel3.question: Jarrah looks at a pie chart of government spending. Which question best fits a clear reading?
toLevel3.correct: Which service takes the largest slice and which takes the smallest slice in this year's pie chart?
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Asking which service takes the largest and smallest slices fits a clear pie chart reading.

distractors.answer: What is the colour of every chart on every wall in every classroom in every school in any year?
distractors.explanation: Wall chart colours have no link to spending shares on a pie chart.

distractors.answer: How many leaves fall outside the school during the autumn months across a stretch of ten whole years?
distractors.explanation: Falling leaves have no link to spending shares on a pie chart.

toLevel3.question: Anika reads a line graph that shows more people working from home each year for five years. What does the line graph reveal?
toLevel3.correct: An upward trend in working from home across the five years on the line graph
toLevel3.correctExplanation: A line that climbs each year for five years reveals an upward trend in working from home.

distractors.answer: A downward trend in working from home across the five years on the line graph
distractors.explanation: A climbing line shows an upward trend, not a downward one.

distractors.answer: No change in working from home across the five years on the line graph
distractors.explanation: A climbing line shows change, not no change.

toLevel3.question: Sam wants to use a simple supply-and-demand model to explain a price rise. Which idea best fits the topic?
toLevel3.correct: A price often rises when demand grows quickly and supply does not grow at the same pace
toLevel3.correctExplanation: A price often rises when demand outpaces supply, which fits the simple model.

distractors.answer: A price never changes when demand grows because supply always matches demand at every moment
distractors.explanation: Supply does not always match demand at every moment in a market.

distractors.answer: A price always falls when demand grows because supply always grows faster than demand each time
distractors.explanation: Supply does not always grow faster than demand; that is not how the model works.

toLevel3.question: Lila is comparing population line graphs for two countries. Which step best supports a clear comparison?
toLevel3.correct: Look at where the two lines rise, fall, or flatten and note where the patterns agree and differ
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Comparing where the two lines rise, fall, or flatten supports a clear graph comparison.

distractors.answer: Look at the page colour each graph is printed on with no link to any line or any data
distractors.explanation: Page colour has no link to the patterns in a line graph.

distractors.answer: Refuse to look at either line graph and decide that the two countries must have identical patterns
distractors.explanation: Refusing to look at the graphs is the opposite of comparison.

toLevel3.question: Kofi reads about employment changes in a news article. Which approach best supports finding a trend?
toLevel3.correct: Look for repeated direction across many years rather than focusing on a single one-off value
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Looking for repeated direction across many years is the right approach to finding a trend.

distractors.answer: Look for the brightest colour in the article rather than at any value reported in the text
distractors.explanation: Article colour has no link to identifying a trend in employment data.

distractors.answer: Refuse to read the article and decide that no trend can be found in any economic data ever
distractors.explanation: Refusing to read articles is the opposite of finding a trend in them.

toLevel3.question: Yen reads a line graph that drops steadily over five years. What does the graph reveal about the value being measured?
toLevel3.correct: The value has gone down each year across the five years on the line graph
toLevel3.correctExplanation: A steadily dropping line reveals that the value has gone down each year.

distractors.answer: The value has gone up each year across the five years on the line graph
distractors.explanation: A dropping line shows a fall, not a rise.

distractors.answer: The value has stayed the same each year across the five years on the line graph
distractors.explanation: A dropping line shows change, not no change.

toLevel3.question: Rosa wants to predict what employment may look like in a few years. Which step best supports her prediction?
toLevel3.correct: Spot the trend in recent years and use the direction to suggest a likely path forward
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Spotting the recent trend supports a likely prediction for years ahead.

distractors.answer: Spot a single one-off value and treat it as the answer for every year ahead with no trend
distractors.explanation: A one-off value cannot stand in for a trend; trends use many values.

distractors.answer: Refuse to read any graph and decide that prediction has no link to any economic data ever
distractors.explanation: Refusing to read graphs is the opposite of using data for prediction.

toLevel3.question: Amir reads a bar graph and notices that prices have risen each year for ten years. Which idea best fits the pattern?
toLevel3.correct: A clear upward trend in prices across the ten years that the bar graph displays in full
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Year-on-year price rises across ten years fit a clear upward trend.

distractors.answer: A clear downward trend in prices across the ten years that the bar graph displays in full
distractors.explanation: Rising prices each year are an upward trend, not a downward one.

distractors.answer: No change in prices across the ten years that the bar graph displays in full each time
distractors.explanation: Rising prices each year show change, not no change.

toLevel3.question: Jade is comparing two pie charts of government spending across two different years. Which step best supports a clear comparison?
toLevel3.correct: Compare the largest slices in each chart and note which services have grown or shrunk between the years
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Comparing the largest slices and noting growth or shrinkage supports a clear comparison.

distractors.answer: Compare border colour on each chart with no link to any slice or any service
distractors.explanation: Border colour has no link to the spending shares on a pie chart.

distractors.answer: Refuse to read either pie chart and decide that the two years must have identical spending shares
distractors.explanation: Refusing to read the charts is the opposite of comparison.

toLevel3.question: Linh reads a short paragraph about employment in her area. Which approach best supports finding a trend in the text?
toLevel3.correct: Look for repeated direction in the years described and the values quoted in the paragraph
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Looking for repeated direction across the years and values supports finding a trend in text.

distractors.answer: Look for the longest sentence and treat it as the trend with no link to any value or year
distractors.explanation: Sentence length does not show a trend; values across years do.

distractors.answer: Refuse to read the paragraph and decide that text has no link to any trend in any data ever
distractors.explanation: Refusing to read text is the opposite of finding a trend in it.
